rows.title: Basic Accounting I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Analyze five dissimilar business transactions in a double-entry accounting system and prepare general journal entries to record.
objectives: Identify and properly use basic accounting terminology.
State the fundamental accounting equation in the T-account format and label the debit, credit, plus and minus sides.
Analyze business transactions using the rules of debit and credit in a double-entry accounting system and record in the appropriate journal.
Post from the journal to the general ledger.
Prepare three basic financial statements: balance sheet, income statement, statement of owner’s equity.
Journalize and post adjusting, closing, and reversing entries.
Reconcile a bank statement and prepare and record journal entries for the reconciling items.
Prepare and record journal entries to establish and maintain a petty cash fund.
Calculate employee earnings, determine deductions from gross pay, and calculate net pay. Prepare journal entries to record payroll.
Analyze and record sales and purchase transactions of a merchandising business under both periodic and perpetual inventory systems.
Understand and properly use the sales, purchases, cash receipts and cash payments special journals.

rows.title: Horsemanship
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Demonstrate basic handling of the horse including catching, haltering, leading, and tying.
Demonstrate and discuss basic horse care including feeding, parasite control, and stable management.
objectives: Define and demonstrate the correct use of horse terminology.
Identify the most desirable horse for a particular purpose based on the criteria for use. This could include: work, pleasure, and sport.
List performance traits to be considered when selecting horses for a particular purpose.
Outline a plan for basic horse care, including feeding, parasite control, and stable management.
Identify and explain the function and maintenance of various tack.
Demonstrate the appropriate grooming technique for a horse.
Demonstrate proper saddling and bridling techniques with an emphasis on safety.
Demonstrate the proper seat position in the saddle.
List and discuss safety rules and procedures for proper horse care and management.
Identify proper aids, control, and horse schooling techniques.

rows.title: Human Anatomy
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Identify gross and microscopic anatomy and explain interactions of the major organ systems of the body.
Interrelate structure and function at the various levels of organization in the human body.
Define and apply medical terminology associated with the study of human anatomy.
Apply an understanding of anatomy to describe changes that occur with disease, trauma, and aging.
objectives: Identify cellular structures and explain their respective functions.
Describe the basic tissues of the body and their location and outline their functions.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the integumentary system.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the skeletal system.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the muscular system and outline their functional roles in body movements.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the nervous system and outline their functional roles in communication, control, and integration.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the eye and ear and explain their functional roles in vision, hearing and equilibrium.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the endocrine system. List the major hormones, their target organs and effects.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the cardiovascular system and outline their transport roles.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the lymphatic system.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the respiratory system and explain their functional roles in breathing/ventilation.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the digestive system and explain their functional roles in digestion and absorption.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the urinary system and explain their functional roles.
Identify and describe the major gross and microscopic anatomical components of the reproductive system and explain their functional roles in reproduction and inheritance.
Describe the anatomical changes that occur in a limited number of disease states.
Outline the development of the major body systems, and the normal changes that occur with aging.

rows.title: Vehicle Electrical Systems
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Analyze and diagnose an electrical circuit. Determine if the circuit is normal, shorted to power, shorted to ground, or open.
objectives: General Electrical Principles
Define current, voltage and resistance.
Define the two theories of current flow.
Define Ohm's Law.
Define semiconductors and diodes.
Define series and parallel circuits.
Perform troubleshooting on electrical circuits.
Perform troubleshooting with voltmeter, ohmmeter, and ammeter.
Explain and discuss voltage drop testing.
Battery Diagnosis and Service
Explain battery state-of-charge test; determine needed service.
Explain battery capacity (load, high-rate discharge) test; determine needed service.
Explain how to maintain or restore electronic memory functions.
Explain how to inspect, clean, fill, and replace a battery.
Discuss slow and fast battery charging.
Explain how to inspect and clean battery cables, connectors, clamps and hold-downs.
Discuss how to start a vehicle using jumper cables with a battery or auxiliary power supply.
Starting System Diagnosis and Repair
Discuss and explain starter current draw testing.
Discuss inspecting and testing starter relays and solenoids.
Explain how to remove and reinstall a starter.
Discuss starter bench testing.
Explain how to inspect, test, and replace switches.
Evaluate a starter control circuit.
Charging System Diagnosis and Repair
Discuss and explain charging system diagnosis.
Discuss drive belt replacement and inspection.
Discuss voltage regulator testing and evaluation.
Explain alternator replacement procedures.
Discuss undercharging, no-charge, and overcharge conditions.

rows.title: Mandarin Chinese 1
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.

Students will give an oral presentation in class, including a brief conversation with a classmate and/or the instructor which includes responding to oral questions. Student performance will be evaluated according to a grading rubric.

Students will demonstrate written proficiency on a variety of topics based on course work and the course objectives which will appear on the final exam.  Success will be measured by the instructor in the form of a percentage of correct answers or by evaluation according to an appropriate grading rubric.
objectives: Discuss, in Chinese, the culture of Chinese speakers in China and around the world, including home, holidays, education, foods, and leisure activities.
Ask and answer questions in Chinese.
Pronounce Chinese words and phrases with 70% accuracy and understandable to a sympathetic ear.
Write a selected set of core characters in Chinese, with a high degree of accuracy.
Present an oral report describing oneself in Chinese and understandable to a sympathetic ear.
Produce a letter or description of self, personal history, work experiences, or goals for the future in Chinese.
Answer questions verbally about themselves and their immediate environment in Chinese.

Demonstrate comprehension of information in ads, schedules, weather reports, biographies, dates, and times with a level of accuracy consistent with ACTFL standards for novice learners and relate that information verbally and in writing.
Read from a selected list of Chinese words with 80% accuracy.

rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

Anatomic Structures:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to determine the sequence of development of embryologic development of structures found within the head and demonstrate their mastery locating critical anatomic structures of periodontium and teeth.
objectives: Identify the surface anatomy of the face and neck.
Apply general and specific anatomic terms to the orofacial region.
Explain the embryologic development of the fetus.
Recognize the unique histology of the oral region.
Discuss dental anatomy.
Explain morphology and function of teeth.
Define occlusion.
Explain tooth eruption.

rows.title: Beginning ESL
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Write Paragraph:  Write a paragraph of 5 to 7 sentences on a familiar topic.
Read and Interpret Passage:  Read and interpret a narrative or descriptive passage of at least 200 words.

Talk and Communicate Successfully:  Talk for 1 1/2 minutes or longer and communicate successfully. The student can discuss his or her daily schedule, a personal event, a class reading or another topic deemed appropriate by the instructor.
objectives: Comprehend simple face-to-face conversations using previously learned material in pair and group oral and written contexts.
Orally produce simple statements and questions based on personal experiences or familiar material with 70% accuracy.
Interpret dialogues and short, adapted paragraphs drawn from previously learned vocabulary and structures in textbook assignments and on exams.

Use appropriate vocabulary related to day-to-day adult “survival” situations or life skills in areas such as housing, transportation, job safety, emergencies, and general health, both orally and in writing.
Respond appropriately to language that differentiates between past and present events, both orally and in writing.

rows.title: Exploring the Humanities
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Analyze themes, connections, historical context, and ideas in the various areas of the Humanities, including but not limited to: visual arts, music, literature, and philosophy.
Examine three major works in the humanities from different cultures, compare and contrast the ways in which these works express the human experience.
Analyze past cultural achievements in the context of present-day intellectual expressions.
Identify and contrast the differences between primary and secondary sources.
objectives: Explain what the humanities are and how they relate to each other.
Analyze in a detailed way a portion of the expressive works of humankind.

Examine, comprehend, and identify major works in the humanities. Write and discuss those works in the context of the proper historical period and with an appreciation of other expressions from different humanities areas produced in the same environment.

rows.title: Microbiology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Aseptic Techniques:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to properly use aseptic techniques for the transfer and handling of microorganisms and instruments.
Methods:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to use appropriate microbiological media and analytical methods to identify a specific bacterial species.
Interpret:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to interpret a sequence of genetic code.
Scientific Skills: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to use scientific inquiry skills related to hypothesis, prediction, assumption, interpretation and evaluation.
objectives: List significant microbiologists and describe their notable scientific contributions.
Discuss methods of taxonomy.
Handle live microbes with safe aseptic technique skills.
Demonstrate understanding of the scientific method by performing controlled ecperiments and analyzing the results.
Inoculate sterile media with live microbes and analyze their subsequent growth.
Prepare wet mounts and smears of microbial samples.
Demonstrate a number of differential microbial stains, including the Gram stain, acid fast stain, endospore stain, and capsule stain.
Compare and contrast typical eukaryotic and prokaryotic cell structure and function.
Discuss atypical bacteria such as Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Mycobacterium and Mycoplasma.
Compare and contrast bacteria, viruses and prions.
Identify metabolic pathways and types of metabolism, including cellular respiration, fermentation, anaerobic respiration, and photosynthesis.
Compare different types of enzymes and enzyme regulatory mechanisms.
Recognize the different categories of organic compounds and discuss their role in living cells.
Discuss in detail the replication of bacterial DNA.
Contrast different types of mutations and their effects to the individual and the population.
List different types of genetic transfer in bacteria.
Discuss in detail transcription and translation in prokaryotic cells.
Describe the lytic and lysogenic cycles of viruses.
Describe the theory and practice of modern biotechology procedures, including gel electrophoresis, immunoblotting, polymerase chain reaction, recombination, and gene therapy.
Compare and contrast the significant features of specific and non-specific immunity.
Discuss the signs, symptoms, pathogenesis and treatment of certain microbial diseases.
Recognize typical epidemiological patterns.
Describe the role of microbes in the environment, medicine, and industry.
rows.objectives_lead: Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to:

rows.title: Physical Science Survey
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Information Recall:  Recall essential factual material pertinent to the objectives and content of the course.
Apply Knowledge and Skills to Solve Problems:  Apply knowledge and skills derived from mastery of the course objectives to solve problems.
objectives: Describe the scientific method.
Perform measurements of quantities such as length, mass, and volume.
Apply Newton’s Laws of motion to simple situations; distinguish between mass and weight; and explain how action and reaction forces are related to each other.

Use the definitions of momentum, work, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy and the relationship between net force, work, and kinetic energy to solve problems involving conservation of energy and momentum.
Relate impulse to momentum change and work to changes in mechanical energy.

Using Newton’s Law of Gravity, explain the meaning of an inverse square force law, describe how satellites are placed into orbit, and describe why astronauts feel weightless in an orbiting spacecraft.
Applying the definitions of pressure and density, explain why pressure increases with depth in a fluid and how this gives rise to buoyancy, and apply Archimedes’ principle.

Distinguish between heat, temperature and thermal energy as distinct concepts. Use specific heat to relate heat transfer to temperature change, describe the role of heat transfer in phase changes, and identify the mechanism(s) responsible for heat transfer in a given situation.

State the law describing forces between electric charges. Distinguish between voltage and current, apply the definitions of voltage, current and resistance, and apply these ideas to predict the behavior of simple series and parallel circuits.

Describe periodic wave motion, in terms of amplitude, period, wavelength, and frequency. Distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves; describe reflection, refraction, and interference of waves. Distinguish between traveling and standing waves, and describe simple standing wave patterns in one dimension.
Describe the properties of sound, explain the Doppler effect, and solve simple problems involving sound.
Describe electromagnetic radiation, interpret the electromagnetic spectrum, and describe sources of light.
Describe how the color of an object depends on the color of the light used to illuminate it and describe how images are formed by mirrors and lenses.
Describe and interpret the characteristics of the atomic, molecular and ionic classes of matter and identify the class to which substances belong.
Describe the characteristics of the phases of matter and the connections between the properties using the particle model.
Classify substances as elements, compounds, or mixtures.
Identify processes as physical or chemical changes.

Explain the roles of protons, electrons, and neutrons in atomic structure and apply the definitions of atomic number and mass number. Describe the experimental evidence for the nuclear model of the atom. Describe and apply the electron energy level/shell model of electronic structure.

Explain the historical organization of elements in the periodic table according to patterns in chemical and physical properties and explain the modern organization of the periodic table according to electronic structure.
Draw Lewis dot structures of atoms, ions, and simple molecules.
Distinguish between ionic and covalent bonds and define and interpret electronegativity. Describe how polarity of bonds/molecules affects properties such as solubility and boiling point.
Define and apply the mole concept and convert between weight and moles for quantities of elements and compounds.
Use chemical equations to describe reactions, balance simple chemical equations, and relate amounts of reactants and products in terms of numbers of particles and mass.
Classify chemical reactions according to type and interpret simple reactions of the various types (precipitation, oxidation-reduction, acid-base/neutralization).
Describe and interpret energy changes during chemical reactions and identify factors that affect reaction rate. Identify and interpret factors that affect if a reaction will occur.

Interpret the basic concept of chemical equilibrium and apply this to simple situations including acids and bases (distinguishing between strong and weak acids and bases), and explain and interpret pH.
Identify some of the most common functional groups and name and draw structures for simple hydrocarbons, alcohols, and other organic compounds. Identify and interpret structural isomers.
Define radioactivity, describe types of radioactive decay, define and apply half-life, interpret the mass-energy relationship, and describe nuclear fission and fusion.

rows.title: Sociology of Mass Media
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Theoretical Approaches:  Compare the various theoretical approaches to the study of mass media.
Key Role of Mass Media:  Describe the key role the mass media play in shaping and organizing public discourse, social stratification, and social structure.
Societal Effects of Mass Media:  Compare the individual versus societal effects of mass media.
Mass Media & Social Institutions:  Evaluate the nature of the relationship between mass media and social institutions including the economy and government.
Structure/Organization:  Explain the structure and organization of mass media.
Audience:  Describe the role of “the audience” as consumers of mass media.
objectives: Discuss the significance of mass media in a contemporary, democratic society and how this compares globally.
Analyze the role that media plays in shaping and organizing public discourse.
Describe and compare the key theoretical perspectives in the study of mass media.
Compare and contrast the role of media in a cross cultural context.
Critically analyze cultural consumption of media including the construction of meaning and sub cultural resistance.
Explain what is meant by "media power" and the relationship of this term to issues of ownership and control.
Analyze the role mass media plays in the creation, persistence, and disruption of social inequality.
